column2: definition
column3: other meaning (only when the word means something else elsewhere)

column2: The time and memory a classical computer needs to reproduce a quantum computation. It is the bar a quantum advantage claim must beat.
The problem size at which a quantum computer starts to outperform the best classical method, including all overheads.
A proven gap in which the best classical method needs exponentially more resources than the quantum one, as with Shor's algorithm for factoring.
The point, often put at around 50 good qubits, at which a quantum device can perform a task no classical supercomputer can reproduce in reasonable time.
A quantum computer producing reliable results at a scale beyond brute-force classical simulation, useful for research, even if faster classical approximations may exist.
The size and quality at which a quantum computer first reaches quantum utility, typically put at about 100 qubits running deep circuits reliably.
The computing effort for a tensor-network method to simulate a quantum circuit, which grows with the entanglement the circuit creates.
How much faster a quantum approach reaches a solution of given quality compared with a classical one, measured in real time.
An experiment run on a quantum computer at a size beyond brute-force classical simulation, such as IBM's 127-qubit experiment in 2023.
A fidelity estimate from cross-entropy benchmarking, which compares measured outputs of random circuits with their ideal probabilities. It was used in quantum supremacy experiments.
For an optimization algorithm, the value of the solution found divided by the best possible value. For QAOA, a ratio close to 1 means near-optimal answers.
A quantity describing how tightly values, such as gradients or kernel values, cluster around their average. Strong concentration signals barren plateaus.
How quickly an optimization or algorithm approaches its final answer as iterations increase.
The difference between the cost a variational algorithm reaches and the true optimum, a measure of how well it has converged.
A measure of a model's capacity, how many independent directions its parameters can explore, used to compare quantum and classical learning models.
The difference between an estimated energy, for example from VQE, and the exact value. Chemical accuracy requires about 1.6 millihartree.
The spread of gradients of a variational circuit over random parameters. If it shrinks exponentially with qubit number, the circuit has a barren plateau.
How good an answer an algorithm returns, for example how close an optimization result is to the true optimum.
The number of helper qubits a circuit needs beyond those holding the data.
The number of layers of gates in a circuit when gates that can run at the same time are grouped. Deeper circuits suffer more noise.
The number of qubits a circuit uses, including ancillas. Together with depth, it describes the size of a circuit.
The number of Clifford gates in a circuit. These are cheap on fault-tolerant hardware, unlike non-Clifford gates.
The total number of gates in a circuit, a basic measure of its size and cost.
The number of layers in a circuit, where each layer contains gates that act in parallel.
The number of gates after compiling a circuit into a device's native gate set, which reflects its real cost on that device.
The number of non-Clifford gates, such as T or Toffoli, in a circuit. It drives the cost of fault-tolerant computation.
The number of T gates in a circuit. Since T gates are the expensive part of fault-tolerant computing, minimizing it is a major goal.
The number of two-qubit gates in a circuit. They are usually the noisiest gates, so this count strongly predicts errors.
How long a qubit keeps its quantum information before noise destroys it, usually described by T1 and T2.
The best fidelity a gate could reach if its only errors came from the qubit's finite T1 and T2 during the gate.
T2: the time over which a qubit loses phase coherence between |0⟩ and |1⟩. It includes both energy relaxation and pure dephasing.
T2*: the coherence time measured by a Ramsey experiment without refocusing, including slow noise and inhomogeneities. It is usually shorter than T2.
column3: In NMR, free-induction decay is the signal emitted by nuclear spins after a pulse.

column2: A technique that applies a π pulse halfway through free evolution to refocus slow noise, giving a longer coherence time T2E. It is also the name of that measurement.
The spectral width of a transition set by processes affecting every emitter or qubit equally, such as its own decay and dephasing.
Widening of a spectral line because different emitters or repetitions have slightly different frequencies, for example from their environments.
How long a quantum memory can store a state with acceptable fidelity.
Tφ: the dephasing time that comes only from frequency fluctuations, excluding energy loss. It satisfies 1/T2 = 1/(2T1) + 1/Tφ.
A measure of how slowly a resonator or qubit loses energy: its frequency times its energy lifetime (Q = ωT1). Higher Q means lower loss.
column3: In engineering generally, the Q factor describes the damping of any oscillator.

column2: T1: the average time for a qubit in |1⟩ to decay to |0⟩ by losing energy. It sets an upper limit on coherence.
T1ρ: the relaxation time of a qubit while it is continuously driven, which reveals noise at the drive's Rabi frequency.
The coherence time measured with a Hahn echo sequence, which removes slow noise. It is usually longer than T2*.
The ability of any qubit to interact directly with any other, as in trapped ions. It avoids the SWAP gates needed on sparse layouts.
How many qubit pairs can interact directly, relative to all possible pairs. Denser maps need fewer SWAPs.
The number of qubits each qubit can interact with directly. Higher degree makes routing easier but increases crosstalk.
The largest number of steps needed to connect any two qubits on a device's coupling graph. It bounds how far qubits may need to be moved.
The number of error-corrected logical qubits a device can provide.
A layout in which each qubit interacts only with those next to it, common in superconducting chips.
The number of hardware qubits in a device, which says little about its power without quality measures.
The number of qubits in a device or circuit, the most quoted but often least informative quality measure.
The extra gates, mostly SWAPs, added to move qubits next to each other on hardware with limited connectivity.
The number of extra SWAP gates a circuit needs to fit a device's connectivity, each typically costing three CNOTs.
A distance between quantum states equal to the arccosine of the square root of their fidelity. It measures the angle between them in state space.
A distance between density matrices based on their fidelity. It is related to the quantum Fisher information and is used in geometry of states.
The distance between two quantum channels given by the diamond norm of their difference. It measures how well they can be told apart in the worst case.
A norm on quantum channels that measures worst-case distinguishability, even when the channel acts on part of an entangled state. It is the standard measure for fault-tolerance proofs.
column3: In mathematics, the diamond norm is also called the completely bounded trace norm.

column2: The distance between two matrices given by the square root of the sum of squared differences of their entries. It is simple but not tied to measurement outcomes.
The natural distance on the space of pure quantum states, based on the angle between state vectors. It underlies the quantum natural gradient.
The distance between two matrices, √Tr((A−B)†(A−B)). It is easy to compute and used in circuit compilation and learning.
A symmetric, bounded measure of the difference between two probability distributions, based on their average. It is used to compare measured and ideal outputs.
A measure of how one probability distribution differs from another, the classical version of relative entropy. It is not symmetric.
The distance between two operators given by the largest singular value of their difference, measuring the worst-case effect on any state.
A measure of how distinguishable one state is from another, Tr ρ(log ρ − log σ). It never increases under noise.
The largest difference in probability two distributions can assign to any event, half the sum of absolute differences. It is used to compare output distributions.
The distance between two states, half the trace norm of their difference. It gives the best possible probability of telling them apart with one measurement.
A measure of how much quantum information survives a channel, S(B) − S(RB). It sets the rate for sending qubits through the channel.
A measure of entanglement for two qubits, from 0 for separable states to 1 for maximally entangled ones. It gives the entanglement of formation.
The uncertainty remaining about one system when another is known, S(A|B) = S(AB) − S(B). Unlike the classical case, it can be negative for entangled states.
How many perfect Bell pairs can be extracted per copy of a state using local operations and classical communication, in the limit of many copies.
How many Bell pairs are needed per copy to create a state using local operations and classical communication, in the limit of many copies.
The von Neumann entropy of one part of a pure state, which measures how entangled that part is with the rest.
The average entanglement needed to build a mixed state, minimized over all ways of writing it as a mixture of pure states.
The smallest number of product terms needed to write a state, or its components, which measures how entangled it is. It generalizes the Schmidt rank.
The quantity χ that bounds how much classical information can be extracted from an ensemble of quantum states.
An easily computed entanglement measure based on the partial transpose, log₂ of the trace norm of the partially transposed state.
An entanglement measure based on the negative eigenvalues of the partial transpose. It is non-zero only for entangled states and is easy to compute.
The total correlation between two systems, S(A) + S(B) − S(AB), including both classical and quantum parts.
The probability that a measurement records the wrong state, for example reading |1⟩ as 0.
The average error of a Clifford gate from randomized benchmarking, measured over random Clifford sequences.
The average error of a single gate, often derived from benchmarking.
IBM's measure of average error per two-qubit gate within full layers of gates across a chain of qubits, including crosstalk. It is derived from layer fidelity.
The error rate of a qubit while it waits without being operated on.
The probability per operation that a qubit leaks out of its computational states into higher levels.
The probability that a logical qubit suffers an error during one round of error correction.
The logical error rate per round of syndrome measurement, the same as logical error per cycle.
The middle value of gate errors across a device, often quoted because it is less affected by a few bad qubits than the average.
The probability of getting the wrong result when measuring a qubit.
The average error of one-qubit gates, typically much lower than two-qubit gate error.
The average error of two-qubit gates, usually the largest gate error in a device and a key figure of merit.
The fidelity between a real gate and the ideal one, averaged over all input states. It is what randomized benchmarking estimates.
How close a prepared two-qubit state is to the ideal Bell state, a common test of entangling gates.
The fidelity between two density matrices, (Tr√(√ρ σ √ρ))², also called Uhlmann fidelity. Some authors use it without the square.
How well a channel preserves the entanglement of a system with a reference, measuring how well it transmits quantum information.
A measure from 0 to 1 of how close two quantum states or processes are, where 1 means identical.
column3: In everyday English, fidelity means faithfulness; in audio it means accuracy of sound reproduction.

column2: How close a real gate is to the ideal one, from 0 to 1. Fault-tolerant computing typically needs gate fidelities above about 99%.
How close a prepared state is to the ideal GHZ state, used to show genuine multi-qubit entanglement.
A similarity measure between two probability distributions, (Σ √(p_i q_i))², used to compare measured and ideal outputs.
The fidelity of an operation counted only on the runs a detector marked as successful.
The fidelity of a state or operation on encoded logical qubits after error correction.
How close a gate on error-corrected logical qubits is to the ideal gate.
The fidelity between two density matrices, which may be mixed, given by the Uhlmann formula.
The fidelity between a real process and the ideal one, computed from their Choi states. It relates simply to the average gate fidelity.
The fidelity between two pure states, the squared overlap |⟨ψ|φ⟩|².
How close a prepared state is to a target state, from 0 to 1.
An easily computed lower bound on the Uhlmann fidelity between two states.
An easily computed upper bound on the Uhlmann fidelity between two states.
The standard fidelity between two density matrices, (Tr√(√ρ σ √ρ))², equal to the best overlap between their purifications.
The difference between a qubit's 0→1 and 1→2 transition frequencies. It lets a transmon act as a qubit, and a small value makes leakage easier.
How strongly two quantum systems interact, such as two qubits or a qubit and a resonator, usually given as a frequency. It sets gate speed.
The number of photons in a readout resonator above which the simple dispersive picture breaks down and readout starts to disturb the qubit.
The shift in a resonator's frequency that depends on the qubit's state, written χ. Detecting it is how superconducting qubits are read out.
The amplitude of the field driving a qubit, which sets how fast it rotates (its Rabi frequency).
Two qubits, or two of their transitions, having frequencies close enough to interfere, causing crosstalk and gate errors. It limits fixed-frequency chip yields.
The number of photons in a mode, such as a resonator. Measuring or controlling it matters for readout and bosonic qubits.
The strength of a control pulse, which sets how far it rotates a qubit. It must be calibrated precisely.
The energy difference between a qubit's |0⟩ and |1⟩ states, expressed as a frequency, typically a few gigahertz for superconducting qubits.
The fraction of fabricated qubits that work well enough to use.
column3: In manufacturing generally, yield is the fraction of good products.

column2: The frequency width of a resonator's response, κ, set by how fast photons leak out. It affects readout speed and Purcell decay.
The error rate on qubits that are idle while operations happen nearby, caused by crosstalk.
A qubit that is not part of an operation but may be affected by it, or may affect it, through crosstalk. It can also mean a qubit used only to sense noise.
The strength of the residual ZZ interaction between two qubits, usually in kilohertz. Lower is better when no gate is applied.
The matrix representing a quantum channel, obtained by applying it to half of a maximally entangled state. It fully describes the channel.
How large the systematic, unitary part of a device's error is, which can add up quickly across a circuit.
How large the random, stochastic part of a device's error is.
The smallest number of Kraus operators needed to describe a channel. A rank of 1 means the channel is unitary.
The χ matrix describing a quantum process in a fixed operator basis, such as the Paulis. It is what process tomography reconstructs.
A measure of how close a process is to unitary, 1 for a perfect unitary and lower for noisy processes.
The smallest environment size needed to realize a channel as a unitary followed by discarding the environment. It equals the Kraus rank.
A measure of how much a noise process preserves the purity of states, which separates coherent from incoherent errors. It is measured by purity benchmarking.
How far a device's physical error rate is below the code threshold. The further below, the faster logical errors fall with code size.
The factor by which logical errors fall when the code distance increases, also called the Lambda factor.
The coherence time of an encoded logical qubit, the logical counterpart of a physical qubit's T2.
The number of physical qubits used per logical qubit, or the physical area a qubit takes on a chip.
The product of the number of qubits used and the time they are used, measuring the total resources of a fault-tolerant operation.
The physical error rate below which error correction lowers logical errors as the code grows.
How the average success probability falls with sequence length in randomized benchmarking, used to extract the error per gate.
A randomized benchmarking variant that needs no inverse gate at the end, using random sequences whose ideal output is a single known bit string.
A method that estimates circuit fidelity by comparing measured outputs of random circuits with their ideal probabilities, used in supremacy experiments.
A randomized benchmarking variant that samples random layers of native gates directly, so it scales to more qubits than standard RB.
A randomized benchmarking variant that inserts a specific gate between random Cliffords, to estimate that one gate's error.
IBM's measure of the fidelity of a full layer of gates across many qubits, including crosstalk, from which the error per layered gate is derived.
The linear version of XEB, which estimates fidelity from the average ideal probability of observed bit strings. It is the form used by Google.
A randomized benchmarking method that runs a random circuit and then its mirror image, so the ideal output is known and many qubits can be tested.
A randomized benchmarking variant that measures how purity decays, to separate incoherent errors from coherent ones.
The rate at which success probability falls with sequence length in randomized benchmarking, from which the error per gate is computed.
Running randomized benchmarking on several qubits at once, to measure how crosstalk raises errors compared with isolated runs.
Randomized benchmarking with random Clifford sequences followed by an inverse gate, fitting the exponential decay of survival probability.
One minus the average probability of misreading a qubit's state, a measure of readout quality.
How well a readout can tell apart the signals for |0⟩ and |1⟩, set by how much their distributions overlap.
In superconducting readout, how far apart the signals for |0⟩ and |1⟩ are in the IQ plane compared with their noise, which sets readout fidelity.
How well a measurement leaves the qubit in the state it reported, tested by measuring twice and checking agreement.
The extra shots or processing needed to correct readout errors, which grows with error rates and qubit number.
The probability of reading a qubit's state correctly, averaged over |0⟩ and |1⟩.
The probability of correctly identifying a qubit's state from one measurement, without averaging.
A range that, with a stated probability, contains the true value of an estimated quantity, such as a fidelity.
column3: This is a standard statistics term.

column2: The number of independent samples a set of measurements is worth, which can be lower than the raw count when samples are correlated or weighted.
How much an estimate would vary if the experiment were repeated. It falls as the number of shots grows.
How many times a circuit is run and measured to estimate its results. More shots give more precise estimates.
The number of samples, or state copies, needed to learn something to a given accuracy.
Random variation in results caused by a finite number of shots.
How long it takes to run a circuit once on hardware, including gates and measurement.
How long a single gate takes to perform, from nanoseconds for superconducting qubits to microseconds for trapped ions.
The time taken to perform a gate on hardware, the same as gate duration.
How quickly gates can be performed, the inverse of gate duration. Faster gates allow more operations within coherence time.
How much useful quantum computation a system completes per unit of time, including overheads.
How long it takes to measure a qubit. Long readout slows error correction and leaves more time for errors.
How many times per second an experiment or circuit can be repeated, including reset and measurement.
How many measurement samples per second a system produces.
How many circuit runs a quantum computer completes each second.
The total time needed to reach an answer of required quality, including all repetitions and classical processing.
The real elapsed time a computation takes, as measured by a clock, including all overheads.
A metric, promoted by IonQ, for the largest number of qubits on which a suite of application benchmark circuits run successfully.
Benchmarks that measure performance on circuits from real applications, such as chemistry or optimization, instead of random circuits.
CLOPS: IBM's measure of how many layers of a quantum volume circuit a system runs per second, including classical overheads.
A task used in quantum volume: producing heavy outputs, bit strings with above-median ideal probability, more than two-thirds of the time.
The fraction of measured bit strings that are heavy outputs. It is the pass-or-fail test in the quantum volume benchmark.
A benchmark that runs circuits followed by their mirror images, so the ideal output is known and many circuit shapes can be tested at scale.
A benchmark from Atos that measures the largest Max-Cut problem size for which a quantum computer running QAOA does significantly better than random guessing.
A benchmark proposed by Dong and Lin in 2021, inspired by the classical LINPACK, which tests quantum computers on random linear-algebra problems encoded in circuits.
column3: LINPACK is a classic benchmark used to rank classical supercomputers.

column2: IBM's single-number benchmark: the largest square random circuit (width equals depth) a device can run successfully, reported as 2 to the power of that size.
A benchmark that measures the performance of a combined quantum and classical system, including communication and classical processing.
rQOPS: Microsoft's metric for fault-tolerant machines, counting how many operations per second run on logical qubits at a set low error rate.
A benchmark that tests circuits across a range of widths and depths, mapping which circuit sizes a device can run successfully.
